assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, combine Lamb-Dicke confinement with massively parallel interrogation of neutral atoms. They have pushed fractional frequency uncertainty and stability to the low 10^-18 level, well beyond microwave standards. This is the clearest case where a laser-spectroscopy technique has changed what can be measured and how accurately, and it underlies redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and fundamental-constant searches.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and led the early Sr demonstrations. Ye's JILA group drove the systematic-uncertainty and stability record and the many-body clock. The two-name configuration is clean, though Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already recognised adjacent technologies, and others in the field (Lemonde, Ludlow, Schmidt) could be raised. I would not widen it.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs worldwide (Japan, USA, Germany, France, UK, China) reproduce and surpass each other. Roadmap towards a redefinition of the second is under way. Maturity is high and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether credit should include early Sr lattice experiments from other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto) is not settled from the supplied text.
Overlap with earlier prizes on frequency combs and ion clocks could be argued as reducing novelty.
I am relying on my own recollection of the achieved uncertainties rather than verifying them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters. The superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes turned cold atoms into a controllable quantum simulator for many-body physics. The impact on both atomic physics and condensed-matter theory is broad and durable.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and collaborators) provided the theory proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model in lattices. Bloch and Greiner carried out the Mott-insulator observation and the quantum-gas microscope developments, with Bloch leading the broader programme. Dalibard, Cirac and Hulet/Gross/Bakr are plausible alternates, so the three-name choice leaves real credit disputes that I cannot resolve from the evidence supplied.
assessment.maturity: The field is mature, with many independent groups using the platform and a long record of reproduced results. Timely, though it overlaps with the Bose-Einstein condensation prize (2001) in lineage.
uncertainties: Which of Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Cirac and Dalibard are the decisive contributors is contested.
Overlaps with the separate trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates through Zoller and Cirac.
Quantum-simulation claims of advantage over classical computing are still evolving.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter-wave phase to measure acceleration, rotation and gravity with extreme sensitivity. It brings laser cooling and Raman or Ramsey-Bordé pulses into precision measurement, enabling measurements of the gravitational constant, the fine-structure constant, gravity gradients and tests of the equivalence principle. This is directly in line with the principle that technical progress is bounded by what we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Bordé contributed the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer concept, Pritchard the first demonstrations of atom optics and interferometers with material gratings, and Kasevich (with Chu) the light-pulse Raman gravimeter and gyroscope. Steven Chu was recognised in 1997 for laser cooling but not for the interferometer, and the credit list is a reasonable three-way split, though Chu and Kasevich overlap by publication.
assessment.maturity: Laboratory instruments are mature and commercial gravimeters exist. Space-based and large-baseline experiments are still developing, so some applications are not yet confirmed. Recognition is timely but not urgent.
uncertainties: Credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu and Rasel is not unambiguous.
Fundamental-physics claims (equivalence principle, gravitational waves detectors) have not yet matured.
Not all independent results at the highest precision are fully reconciled (e.g. G and alpha determinations).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions, and the subsequent experimental realisation with entangling gates and algorithms, established a leading route to quantum computing. Ion-trap processors currently have the highest-fidelity gates. The result is conceptually clear and significant.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 theoretical proposal. Blatt's Innsbruck group did the main experimental implementation of gates, teleportation and algorithms. Wineland and Monroe (NIST/Maryland) are also central, and Wineland was already recognised in 2012, which complicates a fair allocation.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation is extensive and independent (Innsbruck, NIST, Maryland, Oxford, Quantinuum). Timing is plausible, but the 2012 prize on single quantum systems reduces the incremental gap.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche) and with B023 and B009 (Cirac and Zoller) creates redundancy.
Monroe and Wineland's contributions to gates are not in the supplied credit list, so allocation is incomplete.
Scalability to fault tolerance remains unproven.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and E91) turned entanglement and the no-cloning property into a concrete protocol with provably secure key exchange. The ideas have driven decades of experiments in quantum optics, from fibre links to satellites, and helped define quantum information science.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard gave BB84 in 1984, and Ekert gave the entanglement-based protocol in 1991. The three-name combination is natural, though Wiesner's conjugate coding earlier and Bell-test experimenters were recognised in the 2022 prize (Aspect, Clauser, Zeilinger), which itself overlaps.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations are numerous and independent, including satellite QKD. Practical device security and deployment issues remain, but the physical idea is firmly confirmed. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Stephen Wiesner (conjugate coding) is not in the credit list.
Partial overlap with the 2022 prize in the entanglement and Bell-test lineage.
The physical-science novelty versus the computer-science and cryptography contribution may be debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres gives room-temperature solid-state spin qubits and nanoscale sensors for magnetic field, temperature and electric field, with applications in biology and materials. The sensing capability extends the reach of measurement, which is the core of my own interest, and the optical-spin interface is close to my work on coherent light-matter interaction in solid-state crystals.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins and coherent control, while Lukin led quantum-register and sensing developments. Others such as Awschalom, Hanson, Walsworth and Lukin's collaborators also made decisive contributions, so the three-name selection excludes important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation is broad across many groups. The sensing applications are partly established and partly still emerging, so the sensing frontier is still moving.
uncertainties: Allocation among Wrachtrup, Jelezko, Lukin, Awschalom, Hanson and Walsworth is contested.
Many sensing applications remain at the proof-of-concept stage.
I declare my own field proximity (solid-state optical coherence) as a potential bias.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED places superconducting artificial atoms in microwave resonators, giving strong coupling, dispersive readout and a platform for modern quantum processors. The conceptual transfer of cavity QED to circuits is elegant and has strong impact.
assessment.attribution: The Yale group (Schoelkopf, Girvin and Blais) proposed and demonstrated circuit QED, with Wallraff's experiment as the first strong-coupling demonstration. Selecting only three out of four excludes Girvin. The 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits recently rewarded the adjacent superconducting-circuit field, which makes a further prize on this topic less urgent.
assessment.maturity: The platform is widely replicated and mature as a scientific tool. However, recognition of this area in 2025 reduces timeliness.
uncertainties: Credit is split among Schoelkopf, Girvin, Blais and Wallraff, and the three-name limit is a real constraint.
Proximity to the 2025 prize reduces the case for the immediate next year.
I rely on my recollection of the 2025 citation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling, trapping and controlling molecules extends laser cooling to complex structure, enabling precision tests such as the electron electric dipole moment, ultracold chemistry and molecular quantum simulation. The experimental difficulty makes the achievement notable.
assessment.attribution: DeMille, Doyle and Ye are credible experimental leaders (laser cooling of molecules, buffer-gas cooling, and Stark-decelerated and polar-molecule work). Others (e.g. Jin, Ni, Meijer, Rempe) made foundational contributions, so the attribution is incomplete and Ye appears also in B046.
assessment.maturity: Rapid progress, but several flagship applications (eEDM bounds aside) are still developing, so the field is somewhat early for recognition.
uncertainties: Foundational contributions by Deborah Jin, Kang-Kuen Ni, Gerard Meijer and others are missing from the credited names.
Quantum-control applications are still demonstrations.
Ye's presence in B046 means the two cannot both be used for the same person.
